To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
living alone, in general, is a negative predictor of wellbeing, whereas living together is a positive predictor of wellbeing.
Living arrangements, in particular intimate partnerships, are a significant factor in personal wellbeing.

1) Living alone and living together are not necessarily mutually exclusive and are often complementary; 2) living alone is not necessarily bad for wellbeing; 3) marriage is good for wellbeing; 4) living apart together is good for wellbeing, and 5) the rise in the number of people living alone is not the same as the rise in the proportion of people living alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the significance of living arrangements for personal wellbeing.
how living arrangements affect wellbeing.
how living alone or together influences wellbeing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
living alone and living together have different impacts on wellbeing depending on the context and culture.
living arrangements are a key factor in determining wellbeing, and that the impact is dependent on cultural and contextual factors.
the wellbeing effects of different living arrangements are complex and context dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
living arrangements are a significant contributor to wellbeing, and the cultural and demographic context is important.
the wellbeing of individuals and communities is enhanced through living arrangements that are culturally acceptable and socially supported.
living arrangements are not necessarily a determinant of wellbeing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
living alone and living together are both significant for wellbeing, but their significance is contextually dependent.
the wellbeing of individuals is strongly related to the living arrangements in which they live, but the nature of that relationship varies across the world.
living arrangements matter for wellbeing.
